title: Observability & Performance
html:
Observability & Performance

Observability is being able to answer questions about a running system that you did not anticipate. Monitoring is checking the ones you did.

The three signals

Metrics - cheap numbers over time. Aggregated, so ideal for dashboards and alerts, useless for explaining an individual request.

Logs - discrete events with context. Expensive at volume, and the place you learn what actually happened.

Traces - one request's path across services, with timing per hop. The only signal that answers "which of these eleven calls was slow".

They complement each other: a metric tells you something is wrong, a trace tells you where, a log tells you why.

Structured logging

Log events with named fields, not interpolated sentences. Order {OrderId} failed after {Attempts} with values attached can be queried - "all failures with more than three attempts" - where a formatted string can only be grepped.

What belongs in a log: a correlation identifier, the operation, the outcome, the duration, and enough identity to find the record. What does not: secrets, tokens, card numbers, personal data beyond what you can justify keeping. Logs are copied to places with weaker access control than your database.

Levels should mean something. Error is "someone must look"; warning is "unexpected but handled"; information is the narrative of normal operation; debug is off in production. Logging everything as error means nobody reads them.

Correlation

One identifier travelling with a request across every service and appearing in every log line. Without it, distributed debugging is a manual join across timestamps. With it, one query returns the whole story. This is the highest-value thing to add to a system that lacks it.

What to measure

The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. If you can only have four dashboards, these.

Latency as percentiles, never an average. An average hides the tail: a p50 of 100ms with a p99 of 4 seconds describes a system that is unusable for one request in a hundred, and its average looks fine. Track p50, p95, p99.

Distinguish saturation from utilisation. A queue depth that keeps growing is saturation, and it means the consumer is permanently too slow - no amount of retrying fixes it.

Finding a performance problem

Measure before changing anything. Intuition about bottlenecks is unreliable, and the cost of optimising the wrong thing is not just wasted effort - it is added complexity in the wrong place.

The usual order of suspicion: a query without an index or in a loop; a network call inside an iteration; work repeated that could be cached; serialisation of large objects; allocation pressure causing collection pauses; a lock serialising work that could be parallel.

Then: reproduce, profile, form a hypothesis, change one thing, measure again. Keep the measurement, because the next person will otherwise re-derive it.

Health checks

Liveness - is the process alive and worth restarting if not. Readiness - can it serve traffic right now, which may be false while a dependency is unavailable. Conflating them causes restart loops: a failing dependency makes liveness fail, the orchestrator restarts a perfectly healthy process, and nothing improves.

Common mistakes

  • Alerting on causes rather than symptoms, producing noise nobody acts on.
  • Averages instead of percentiles.
  • No correlation identifier, so cross-service problems take hours.
  • Secrets or personal data in logs.
  • Optimising without a measurement, then being unable to say whether it helped.
